name: Practice Paper 1
subtitle: RRB Radiographer / X-Ray Technician — Full CBT Mock

subsections.title: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: How many bones are present in the normal adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: An adult skeleton has 206 bones; a newborn has about 270–300 that fuse during growth.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: Which is the largest sesamoid bone of the human body?
questions.explanation: The patella develops within the quadriceps tendon and is the largest sesamoid bone.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: How many vertebrae make up the cervical spine?
questions.explanation: There are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: The 'atlas' is the name given to the:
questions.explanation: C1 is the atlas (supports the skull); C2 is the axis, which carries the dens.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: The sella turcica, which houses the pituitary gland, is a part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The sella turcica is a saddle-shaped depression on the body of the sphenoid bone.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: What is the structural and functional unit of the kidney?
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons, which filter blood and form urine.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung have?
questions.explanation: The right lung has upper, middle and lower lobes; the left lung has two (upper and lower).

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: Which is the longest and strongest bone of the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: Which is the longest part of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: The ileum forms roughly the distal three-fifths of the small intestine; the duodenum is the shortest part.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: Which valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: The mitral valve has two cusps and guards the left atrioventricular opening.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: The floor of the 'anatomical snuffbox' is formed mainly by which carpal bone?
questions.explanation: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a scaphoid fracture, which needs dedicated scaphoid views.

questions.subject: Human Anatomy & Physiology
questions.question: What is the normal lifespan of a red blood cell?
questions.explanation: RBCs survive about 120 days and are then removed mainly by the spleen.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: In which year did Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen discover X-rays?
questions.explanation: Roentgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895 and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: The target of the anode in a general diagnostic X-ray tube is usually made of:
questions.explanation: Tungsten has a high atomic number (74) and a very high melting point (3410 °C), so it is efficient and heat-resistant.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: Approximately what percentage of the electron energy at the target is converted into X-rays in a diagnostic tube?
questions.explanation: About 99% of the electron energy becomes heat; only about 1% becomes X-rays.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: Because of the anode heel effect, X-ray intensity is greater on the:
options: Centre only, falling equally on both sides
questions.explanation: X-rays leaving towards the anode side pass through more target material and are absorbed, so the cathode side is more intense. Place the thicker part of the body under the cathode.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: What is the speed of X-rays in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic waves and travel at the speed of light.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: According to the inverse square law, if the source-to-image distance is doubled, the intensity becomes:
questions.explanation: Intensity ∝ 1/d². Doubling d reduces intensity to (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: A radiograph is correctly exposed at 20 mAs at 100 cm FFD. To keep the same density at 200 cm FFD, the new mAs should be:
questions.explanation: New mAs = old mAs × (new d / old d)² = 20 × (200/100)² = 80 mAs.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: Kilovoltage (kVp) chiefly controls the:
options: Number of electrons emitted by the filament only
questions.explanation: kVp determines photon energy and therefore penetration and radiographic contrast; mAs controls quantity.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: The emission of electrons from the heated filament of an X-ray tube is called:
questions.explanation: Heating the tungsten filament gives electrons enough energy to escape its surface — thermionic emission.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: According to the line focus principle, the effective focal spot is smaller than the actual focal spot because of the:
questions.explanation: The target is angled (typically 7°–20°), so the focal spot projected towards the patient is foreshortened.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: The minimum total filtration recommended for an X-ray tube operating above 70 kVp is:
questions.explanation: At least 2.5 mm Al total filtration (inherent + added) removes soft, low-energy photons that only add to skin dose.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: At diagnostic energies, scattered radiation in soft tissue is produced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Compton scatter dominates in soft tissue at most diagnostic kVp values and is the main source of scatter fog and staff dose.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: The minimum photon energy needed for pair production is:
questions.explanation: Two electron rest masses (2 × 0.511 MeV) are needed, so pair production does not occur at diagnostic energies.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: Grid ratio is defined as:
options: Number of lead strips per cm
Distance between strips ÷ height of strips
Height of the lead strips ÷ distance between the strips
Thickness of lead ÷ thickness of interspace
questions.explanation: Grid ratio = h/D. A higher ratio removes more scatter but needs more exposure and accurate centring.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: What is the SI unit of absorbed dose?
questions.explanation: 1 Gy = 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram. The sievert is for equivalent/effective dose.

questions.subject: Radiation Physics & X-ray Equipment
questions.question: Characteristic X-rays are produced when:
options: An electron is slowed down by the attraction of the nucleus
A photon is completely absorbed by a free electron
An electron and a positron annihilate each other
An incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron and an outer-shell electron fills the vacancy
questions.explanation: The energy difference between the shells is released as a characteristic photon. Slowing near the nucleus gives Bremsstrahlung.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: What is the standard focus-to-film distance (FFD) for a routine PA chest radiograph?
questions.explanation: A long FFD of 180 cm reduces magnification of the heart and gives a sharper image.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: A routine PA chest radiograph is exposed at:
questions.explanation: Full inspiration lowers the diaphragm and shows about 10 posterior ribs above it. Expiration films are taken only for special cases such as pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The occipitomental (Waters) view best demonstrates the:
questions.explanation: In Waters view the petrous ridges are projected below the maxillary sinuses, so the antra are seen clearly.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The occipitofrontal 15° (Caldwell) view mainly demonstrates the:
questions.explanation: Caldwell projects the petrous ridges into the lower third of the orbits, showing the frontal sinuses and anterior ethmoid cells.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The AP axial (Towne's) projection with 30° caudal angulation demonstrates the:
questions.explanation: Towne's view shows the occipital bone, the petrous ridges symmetrically and the dorsum sellae within the foramen magnum.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The submentovertical (SMV) projection is mainly used to demonstrate the:
questions.explanation: SMV (full basal view) shows the skull base, foramina, sphenoid sinus and zygomatic arches.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The line joining the outer canthus of the eye to the centre of the external auditory meatus is the:
questions.explanation: The orbitomeatal line (radiographic baseline) is the reference used for most skull projections.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: Which projection is added to show a suspected scaphoid fracture?
questions.explanation: Ulnar deviation stretches the scaphoid out from behind the other carpals, so the waist is seen without foreshortening.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The AP lordotic chest projection is mainly used to demonstrate the:
questions.explanation: The lordotic position projects the clavicles above the apices, showing apical lesions such as TB.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: To show a small right-sided pleural effusion, the patient is positioned in the:
questions.explanation: Fluid gravitates to the dependent side, so the affected side is placed down. For a pneumothorax the affected side is placed up.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The AP open-mouth projection of the cervical spine demonstrates:
questions.explanation: With the mouth open, the teeth and mandible are moved away from C1–C2, showing the dens.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: The 'Swimmer's' (Twining) projection is used to demonstrate the:
questions.explanation: One arm is raised and the other depressed so that the shoulders do not hide C7–T1 on the lateral view.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: In the oblique lumbar spine projection, the 'neck' of the Scottie dog represents the:
questions.explanation: A break across the neck of the Scottie dog indicates spondylolysis (pars defect).

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: For a suspected fracture of the neck of the femur, the lateral projection of choice is the:
options: Lateral with the leg abducted and externally rotated
questions.explanation: The injured limb is not moved. The frog-leg lateral needs hip abduction and is contraindicated in trauma.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: A patient who cannot stand is suspected of having a pneumoperitoneum. The best projection is the:
questions.explanation: With the left side down, free air rises over the liver, where it is easily seen against the homogeneous liver shadow.

questions.subject: Clinical Radiography — Positioning
questions.question: For an AP projection of the knee, the central ray is directed:
options: To the upper border of the patella
1.25 cm below the apex of the patella
questions.explanation: Centring about 1.25 cm (½ inch) below the patellar apex places the central ray through the knee joint space.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: Which developing agent acts slowly and produces high contrast (dense black areas)?
questions.explanation: Hydroquinone builds up the dense black tones. Metol/Phenidone act quickly and bring out grey detail.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: The clearing (fixing) agent in an X-ray fixer solution is:
questions.explanation: Thiosulphate (hypo) dissolves the unexposed, undeveloped silver halide from the emulsion.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: Which safelight should be used when handling green-sensitive (orthochromatic) film?
questions.explanation: Orthochromatic film is sensitive to blue and green light, so a red filter (e.g., GBX-2) is used. Amber is safe only for blue-sensitive film.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: Which of the following is a rare-earth intensifying screen phosphor?
questions.explanation: Rare-earth phosphors (gadolinium, lanthanum) convert X-rays to light more efficiently than calcium tungstate, so less patient dose is needed.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: The base of a modern radiographic film is made of:
questions.explanation: Polyester is strong, stable and non-flammable. Cellulose nitrate was flammable and is no longer used.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: Geometric unsharpness (penumbra) is reduced by:
options: A smaller focal spot and a smaller object-to-film distance
questions.explanation: Unsharpness = focal spot × OFD / FOD. Use a small focal spot, keep the part close to the film and use a long FFD.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: In computed radiography (CR), the imaging plate is coated with:
questions.explanation: The BaFBr:Eu phosphor stores the latent image, which is released as light when a laser scans the plate.

questions.subject: Image Processing, Darkroom & Image Quality
questions.question: DICOM, the standard used in PACS, stands for:
options: Digital Image Compression of Medical files
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine
Data Integration for Computerised Optical Media
Digital Investigation and Computed Organ Mapping
questions.explanation: DICOM is the international standard for storing and transmitting medical images.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: As per AERB, the effective dose limit for radiation workers is:
options: 50 mSv every year with no averaging
20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (not more than 30 mSv in any single year)
questions.explanation: AERB limits occupational effective dose to 20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 consecutive years, with a maximum of 30 mSv in any one year.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: What is the annual effective dose limit for members of the public?
questions.explanation: The public dose limit is 1 mSv per year.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: The TLD badges issued to radiation workers in India (BARC personnel monitoring) use which phosphor?
questions.explanation: The Indian TLD badge holds three CaSO₄:Dy–Teflon discs under different filters.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: Lead aprons used in diagnostic radiology usually provide a lead equivalence of:
questions.explanation: A minimum of 0.25 mm Pb is required, and 0.35–0.5 mm Pb is commonly used. This stops most scattered radiation.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: The '10-day rule' in radiography applies to:
options: Women of reproductive age, during the 10 days after the onset of menstruation
questions.explanation: Non-urgent abdominal/pelvic exposures are scheduled in the first 10 days of the cycle, when pregnancy is unlikely.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: Which contrast agent is used for a barium meal?
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is insoluble and inert. Soluble barium salts such as the chloride are poisonous.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is the radiographic examination of the:
questions.explanation: HSG shows uterine cavity shape and tubal patency in infertility work-up.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: Which type of contrast medium is used for myelography?
questions.explanation: Only non-ionic agents approved for intrathecal use (e.g., iohexol) are used; ionic agents are neurotoxic intrathecally.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: The first drug given for a severe anaphylactic reaction to contrast media is:
questions.explanation: IM adrenaline 1:1000 (0.5 mg in adults) is first-line, with oxygen, IV fluids and calling the resuscitation team.

questions.subject: Radiation Protection, Contrast & Special Procedures
questions.question: The Seldinger technique is used for:
questions.explanation: Needle puncture → guidewire → needle removed → catheter over the wire. This is the basis of angiography.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: What is the CT number (Hounsfield unit) of water?
questions.explanation: Water is defined as 0 HU and air as −1000 HU; dense cortical bone is about +1000 HU.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: The first clinical CT scanner was developed by:
questions.explanation: Hounsfield built the EMI scanner in 1971–72 and shared the 1979 Nobel Prize with Allan Cormack.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: Clinical MR imaging is based on signals from the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is plentiful in water and fat, and its single proton gives a strong MR signal.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: Which of the following is a classical contraindication to MRI?
questions.explanation: The strong magnetic and RF fields can cause a non-conditional pacemaker to malfunction, move or heat up.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: Diagnostic ultrasound commonly uses a frequency range of:
questions.explanation: Low frequencies (2–5 MHz) penetrate deeper; high frequencies (7–15 MHz) give better resolution for superficial parts.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: Which radionuclide is the most widely used in diagnostic nuclear medicine?
questions.explanation: Tc-99m has a 6-hour half-life and emits 140 keV gamma rays, which suits gamma cameras.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: The anode target commonly used in film-screen mammography is:
questions.explanation: Molybdenum's characteristic X-rays (17–19 keV) give high contrast for soft breast tissue.

questions.subject: CT, MRI, USG, Nuclear Medicine & Patient Care
questions.question: During adult CPR, chest compressions should be given at a rate of:
questions.explanation: Current guidelines: 100–120 compressions/min at a depth of 5–6 cm, with full chest recoil.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: Where is the headquarters of the Northern Railway zone?
questions.explanation: Northern Railway is headquartered at Baroda House, New Delhi.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 between:
questions.explanation: The 34-km run from Bori Bunder to Thane marks the start of Indian Railways.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution deals with:
options: Protection of life and personal liberty
questions.explanation: Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the:
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment added Part IV-A (Article 51A) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which of these states?
questions.explanation: It passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — not Odisha.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: The Battle of Plassey was fought in:
questions.explanation: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey in 1757. Buxar was in 1764 and the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: Which river is known as the 'Dakshin Ganga'?
questions.explanation: The Godavari is the longest river of peninsular India and is called the Dakshin Ganga.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: 23 August, the day Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole, is observed in India as:
questions.explanation: Vikram landed on 23 August 2023, and the date is now observed as National Space Day. National Science Day is 28 February.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: The Durand Cup is associated with which sport?
questions.explanation: The Durand Cup (first held in 1888) is one of the oldest football tournaments in the world.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.question: The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of:
options: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry)
All members of Lok Sabha only
All members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members
Elected members of Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
questions.explanation: Under Article 54, nominated members and members of Legislative Councils do not vote.

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: What is 25% of 480?

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: A train 240 m long passes a signal pole in 12 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: What is the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years?

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: What is the average of the first 10 natural numbers?

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. Working together, they will finish it in:
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per day, so time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: An article bought for ₹400 is sold for ₹460. What is the profit percentage?

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: Find the next number: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ?
questions.explanation: Differences are 5, 7, 9, 11, so the next is +13: 35 + 13 = 48. (Also n² − 1.)

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: If CAT is written as DBU, how is DOG written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one step forward: D→E, O→P, G→H.

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: Pointing to a boy, Rita says, 'He is the son of my father's only son.' How is the boy related to Rita?
questions.explanation: Rita's father's only son is her brother; his son is Rita's nephew.

questions.subject: General Arithmetic, Intelligence & Reasoning
questions.question: Ravi walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right again and walks 5 km. Where is he now from the starting point?
questions.explanation: North 5 and then south 5 cancel out, leaving only the 3 km eastward move.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Pure water is neutral, with [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which cell organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of common salt?
questions.explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is needed for collagen synthesis; its lack causes bleeding gums.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected by using a:
questions.explanation: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina, and a diverging (concave) lens corrects it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which gas is the most abundant in the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere and oxygen about 21%.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A potential difference of 12 V drives a current of 3 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Insulin is secreted by the:
options: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
questions.explanation: Beta cells secrete insulin and alpha cells secrete glucagon.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at −38.8 °C. Gallium melts at about 30 °C, which is above normal room temperature.
